steps.message: Reviewing the intake and the question.

claims.text: Goal: cut electricity bought from the grid by 30% by 2030, on a $600,000 capital budget set for 2027. The baseline is the 284,403 kWh (energy over time) the school buys from the grid each year.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: Efficiency only is estimated to cut 6.2% to 17.6% of annual grid use. That does not reach the 30% goal, but it fits the budget.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Efficiency plus a smaller solar array within budget is estimated to cut 53.6% to 69.7% of annual grid use. It reaches the goal even at the low end and fits the budget, if the roof can carry the array.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: The full path (deeper efficiency, whole-roof solar and a backup battery) is estimated to cover 100% of annual grid use but costs $473,046 to $1,119,287 more than your budget. Meeting the goal at full scale may take more than the amount set aside; whether to extend the budget is your decision once the gap is compared with the savings.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: The goal is a percent cut in electricity, which is the kind of goal modeled here.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: P.S. 38 (R038), an elementary school at 421 Lincoln Avenue, Staten Island, built in 1955, 55,860 sq ft of floor area, flat roof of 34,360 sq ft (your figure), served by Con Edison. The school reports no existing solar, other renewables or efficiency work, so the plan assumes none.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: The city's Local Law 84 energy report (2024) shows 284,403 kWh of electricity, 512,500 kBtu (thousand BTU) of natural gas and 1,476,599.8 kBtu of fuel oil. The electricity figure matches the typed annual use and is treated as measured. Gas and fuel oil heating are outside an electricity goal.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: The city's building footprints show three buildings on the lot, 34,363 sq ft of ground area in total, close to the 34,360 sq ft roof area entered. A footprint is not a measured roof, so the roof area is the user's figure to verify.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: The city record shows no landmark flag for this lot. The owning agency is the Department of Education, so approval runs through DCAS (city building agency), NYC Public Schools or the School Construction Authority (SCA).
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: Flood zone: the current FEMA map shows zone X, an area of minimal flood hazard. Only the flood zone was read; heat and winter-storm ratings were not looked up, and the 2015 preliminary flood map was not checked.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: Solar output range: system losses of 18% (low) to 10% (high) around the solar model's 14% default; weather is typical-year data.
claims.label: ASSUMPTION

claims.text: Usable roof share (setback factor) of 0.55 of the roof area.
claims.label: ASSUMPTION

claims.text: Array density of 66 sq ft per kW (how much power at one moment) of panels.
claims.label: ASSUMPTION

claims.text: Battery size: critical load was not given, so it is estimated at 1.0 W per sq ft x 55,860 sq ft = 55.9 kW (a planning estimate, not metered). Backup length was not given, so 8 hours is assumed. Battery energy = kW x hours / 0.85 round-trip efficiency = 526 kWh.
claims.label: ASSUMPTION

claims.text: Efficiency measures (LED and controls) save 10-20% of annual use. This is a planning estimate, not a cited benchmark and not a building model.
claims.label: ASSUMPTION

claims.text: Benchmark prices and savings percents behind every scenario are planning-level, not quotes: solar $2,528-3,752 per kW and battery $546-812 per kWh (the middle half of similar completed NYC projects, NYSERDA data), efficiency savings of 10-20% (standard) and 15-25% (deep) as planning estimates, with only 62%-88% of efficiency savings counted because the City's audited projects delivered that share.
claims.label: ASSUMPTION

claims.text: The baseline is the 284,403 kWh a year the building buys from the grid. No existing solar or efficiency work is reported, so none was taken into account.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: Efficiency measures such as LED lighting and building controls are assumed to save 10-20% of annual use; the lighting type and controls were not given, so LED is treated as an open measure to confirm. The 10-20% is a planning estimate.
claims.label: ASSUMPTION

claims.text: Only 62% to 88% of predicted efficiency savings is counted, because the City's own audited projects delivered that share (Local Law 87 report, DCAS fiscal year 2022). With that trim, a standard package is estimated to cut 17,633 to 50,055 kWh a year.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Heating is by natural gas and fuel oil, so most of the building's energy is outside an electricity goal.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: Usable roof is estimated at 18,898 sq ft after setbacks, from the 34,360 sq ft roof area entered.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: A whole-roof array is estimated at 286.3 kW DC (direct current).
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: The whole-roof array is estimated to produce 338,147 to 371,605 kWh a year (central 354,876), using a flat-roof tilt of 10 degrees facing south.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: That output is about 119% to 131% of the school's annual use, so the roof could produce more than the building uses. Reduction is capped at 100% and the surplus of 80,194 to 149,771 kWh is not credited, because export credits depend on net-metering rules that were not checked.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Gross value of the whole-roof output at the New York commercial average price is $66,987 to $89,854 a year (central price $0.222 per kWh). This counts every kWh at the retail price, so it overstates savings where output exceeds use.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: City records list the roof as Not Solar Ready, in fair condition and 20 years or more old. The roof may need repair or replacement before solar, so a roofer's survey is needed first.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: Roof area, usable area, pitch, shading and structure are to be verified by an engineer or roofer; the roof area is the user's number.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Scenario A, efficiency only (standard package, no solar): share of goal 21% to 59%, reduction 6.2% to 17.6% of annual use, does not reach the goal. Upfront cost $49,913 to $171,495; net cost the same; simple payback 4.1 to 49.1 years; within budget; no backup power (0 outage hours). Payback is a simple payback, not the full SAM (NREL System Advisor Model) analysis.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Scenario B, efficiency plus 114.2 kW of solar within budget: reduction 53.6% to 69.7% of annual use, reaches the goal (tested at the low end). Upfront cost $338,628 to $600,000; net cost $252,014 to $471,449 after the federal credit counted; simple payback 5.3 to 15.6 years; within budget (56% to 100% of it); no backup power.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Scenario C, deep efficiency, whole-roof solar (286.3 kW) and a 526 kWh battery: reduction 100% of annual use (capped), reaches the goal. Upfront cost $1,073,046 to $1,719,287; net cost $769,732 to $1,268,857 after the federal credit counted; simple payback 11.2 to 22.5 years; over budget; estimated outage backup of 8 to 9.4 hours.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Scenario C costs $473,046 to $1,119,287 more than your budget. It reaches the goal, but meeting it may take more than the amount set aside; compare that gap with the savings before deciding whether to extend the budget.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Annual savings: A $3,493 to $12,103; B $30,212 to $47,943; C $56,340 to $68,769 (only solar that replaces power the school uses is credited).
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Rooftop solar alone could produce about 119% to 131% of annual use, so it more than covers the 30% goal on paper. Efficiency alone does not. The scenario results depend on the roof passing a structural and condition review.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: The budget is a capital budget, and the model treats it as one total upfront figure.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: Scenario B, standard efficiency package: typical range $49,913 to $171,495; the median of similar NYC projects is about $109,211. Based on 42,660 kWh saved a year times $1.17 to $4.02 per kWh saved (the middle half of completed NYC public-sector projects, NYSERDA data). The 10-20% savings figure is a planning estimate.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Scenario B, rooftop solar of 114.2 kW: typical range $288,716 to $428,505; the median of similar NYC projects is about $342,621. Based on $2,528 to $3,752 per kW, the middle half of 239 completed NYC non-residential projects of 100 to 500 kW since 2022 (NYSERDA data).
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Scenario B, federal credit of 30% of solar: $86,615 to $128,551 counted, because the federal elective pay program (direct payment to governmental entities) is listed as open. Solar must be placed in service by 2027-12-31, and whether this school or agency qualifies is not confirmed, so net cost could be higher than shown. Upfront cost without the credit is $338,628 to $600,000.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Scenario B totals: upfront typical range $338,628 to $600,000, median of similar projects about $451,832; net cost $252,014 to $471,449.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Scenario C lines, for comparison: expanded efficiency $62,000 to $217,853 (median about $141,633); solar $723,851 to $1,074,323 (median about $859,000); battery of 526 kWh $287,196 to $427,112 (median about $361,362, from NYC storage projects, NYSERDA data); federal credit of $303,314 to $450,430 counted.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Left out of net cost: the NYC Solar Schools program (DCAS, NYPA and NYC Public Schools solar under power purchase agreements) is uncertain; it is not known whether this building is in the pipeline, so ask DCAS or the SCA. Retrieved 2026-10-19.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: Left out of net cost: the NY-Sun commercial solar incentive is uncertain, because its current block status could not be read from the official page. Check the NYSERDA dashboard in a browser. Retrieved 2026-10-19.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: NYC's sustainable roof rule (Local Laws 92 and 94 of 2019) is a rule, not an incentive: a roof undergoing certain major renovations must carry solar, a green roof or both. A roof replacement before solar could trigger it.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: None of the cost totals include replacing or repairing the roof. The roof is 20 years or more old and rated fair, so a roofer's quote is needed.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Phase 0, confirm data and budget: gather 12 months of bills, confirm the capital budget year (2027) and that $600,000 is a one-time total, and confirm the Con Edison tariff on a bill. Confirm the roof area and the year the roof was last replaced.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Phase 1, professional reviews: a licensed structural engineer (PE) or registered architect (RA) analysis of the roof, plus a roof condition survey and a roofer's quote for repair or replacement. The roof cannot be certified from these records.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Phase 2, efficiency measures: an energy audit, then LED lighting and building controls as confirmed by the audit, which are estimated to cut 6.2% to 17.6% of grid use.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Phase 3, permits and interconnection: DOB permits, a licensed electrician, FDNY rooftop access review, the Con Edison interconnection application, and the DCAS, NYC Public Schools or SCA approval route. Ask DCAS or the SCA whether the Solar Schools program covers this roof.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Phase 4, solar installation: start with the roughly 114 kW array that fits the budget, in service before 2027-12-31 if the federal direct payment is to be pursued. Decide whether to extend the budget for the whole-roof array after comparing the gap with savings.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Phase 5, battery, commissioning and verification: add the backup battery if outage backup for emergency lighting and communications is wanted, then check results against 12 months of bills.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Scenario C is estimated to carry the critical loads for 8 to 9.4 hours in an outage. The critical loads are emergency lighting and communications.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Scenarios A and B give no backup power. Solar panels shut off in an outage without a battery.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Battery sizing of 55.9 kW and 526 kWh is a planning estimate, because the critical load and backup hours were not given: the load is estimated at 1.0 W per sq ft and 8 hours is assumed. A metered critical load would change the size.
claims.label: ASSUMPTION

claims.text: The FEMA effective map shows minimal flood hazard (zone X), so no flood-zone review is triggered. Only the flood zone was read.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: Structural PE or RA analysis of the roof is required before any solar design. The roof cannot be certified from these records.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Roof condition survey and a roofer's quote, because city records show the roof as Not Solar Ready, fair, and 20 years or more old.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Licensed electrician for the design and installation, FDNY review of rooftop access, and a Con Edison utility interconnection review and application. Links are in the contact list at the end.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Because the owner is the Department of Education, the approval route is through DCAS, NYC Public Schools or the SCA. The contact list at the end has the links.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: No landmark flag and no parkland flag appear in the city record, so a Landmarks Preservation Commission review and parkland review are not triggered.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: Electricity can be covered by rooftop solar on paper, but the building also burns natural gas and fuel oil for heat, so net-zero energy would need heating electrification, which is outside this plan.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Learning resource: the city's Local Law 84 energy reports and Local Law 24 solar-readiness records for this building, linked in the sources.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Savings use the New York commercial average electricity price of $0.1981 to $0.2418 per kWh, not this building's own tariff. The tariff must be confirmed on a bill. Con Edison lists several general-service tariffs for NYC, effective 2025-02-01, and none is chosen here.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: The incentive list is a curated register kept by a person, with each official page re-read on 2026-10-19. The federal credit is counted as open, but eligibility is not confirmed. The Solar Schools program and NY-Sun are uncertain and left out of net cost.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: Missing answers: the year the roof was replaced, lighting type, controls, heating and cooling, critical load, backup hours and electricity price. Confidence is lower for claims that depend on them. The plan assumes no existing solar or efficiency work.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: Only the flood zone was read. Heat and winter-storm ratings were not looked up and the 2015 preliminary flood map was not checked.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: The city's tax-lot record lists 17,620 sq ft of building floor area, while the school entered and the Local Law 84 report show 55,860 sq ft. The entered 55,860 sq ft is the working figure; please confirm it.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: All costs and savings are planning ranges, with low confidence. Efficiency savings percents are planning estimates and payback is a simple payback. Nothing here is a promise of savings.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Sources used: the school's intake answers, city building records, Local Law 84 and Local Law 24 data sets, city building footprints, the solar production model, the EIA electricity price, the FEMA flood map, the curated incentive register, and NYSERDA project cost data. Links are in the list at the end.
claims.label: FACT

roadmap.plain_answer: You asked how P.S. 38 can cut electricity bought from the grid by 30% by 2030 on a $600,000 capital budget. The plan estimates that it can, but not with efficiency work alone. Efficiency alone is estimated to cut only 6.2% to 17.6% of grid use, short of the goal. Efficiency plus a smaller rooftop solar array (about 114 kW) is estimated to cut 53.6% to 69.7%, at a typical upfront cost of $338,628 to $600,000, which fits your budget. The whole-roof array plus a backup battery could cover all of your use, but is estimated to cost $473,046 to $1,119,287 more than your budget, so extending it is your decision. The school has no solar or efficiency work today. Limits: city records list the roof as not solar ready and 20 years or more old, and no cost here includes roof repair. The budget option gives no backup power in an outage. Heating fuel is outside this goal. Next steps: have a licensed engineer and a roofer review the roof, and confirm your bills and tariff.
